questions.q: In what year did Kublai Khan formally proclaim the Yuan Dynasty, and what Chinese-era name did he adopt to legitimise his rule?
questions.a: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan Dynasty in 1271 and adopted the era name "Zhiyuan" (至元). A wrong answer (e.g., 1260 when he became Great Khan, or 1279 when the Song fell) reveals confusion between his accession as Mongol Great Khan, the formal dynastic proclamation, and the military completion of the conquest — three distinct political acts.

questions.q: Why did Kublai Khan move the Mongol capital from Karakorum to Dadu (Beijing), and what does this shift reveal about his governing strategy?
questions.a: Kublai moved the capital to Dadu (1264–1267) to position himself within the Chinese agrarian heartland, control the Grand Canal grain supply, and present himself as a legitimate Chinese emperor rather than a steppe overlord. A wrong answer focusing only on "better climate" or "closer to conquests" misses the deliberate political symbolism: Dadu was designed on Chinese cosmological principles (north-south axis, imperial city) to claim the Mandate of Heaven.

questions.q: A Yuan-era edict states: "Mongols and Semu people shall not be tried by Chinese officials; Chinese and Nan people shall not judge Mongols." Using the four-class hierarchy, explain how this legal dualism reinforced Mongol political dominance.
questions.a: The four classes were: (1) Mongols, (2) Semu (Central/West Asians), (3) Han (Northern Chinese, former Jin subjects), (4) Nan (Southern Chinese, former Song subjects). Legal dualism meant the top two classes enjoyed separate courts and lighter punishments, while the bottom two faced harsher Chinese law. This institutionalised ethnic privilege, ensuring Mongol/Semu control over the military and high bureaucracy while using Han/Nan personnel for routine administration — a divide-and-rule tactic that prevented unified Chinese resistance but bred resentment.

questions.q: Compare the Yuan use of paper currency (chao) with the Song Dynasty's earlier monetary experiments. What structural flaw in the Yuan system led to hyperinflation by the 1350s?
questions.a: The Song backed paper money with copper cash reserves and limited issuance; the Yuan made chao inconvertible, issued it without adequate specie backing to fund wars and court expenses, and forbade private metal currency. By the 1350s, over-issuance (estimated 100-fold increase) destroyed trust, causing prices to soar and tax revenue to collapse. A wrong answer blaming "Mongol ignorance of economics" misses the fiscal-military trap: continuous campaigns against Japan, Java, and Burma drained reserves, forcing the print-press solution.

questions.q: Assess the claim: "The Yuan Dynasty's patronage of Tibetan Buddhism (Sakya sect) was purely a religious choice by Kublai Khan." Use evidence of the 'Phags-pa lama relationship and the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs.
questions.a: The claim is false. Kublai's 1260 appointment of 'Phags-pa as Imperial Preceptor and head of the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (Xuanzheng Yuan) created a theocratic-political alliance: the lama provided religious legitimacy (chakravartin ideology) for Mongol rule over Tibet and China, while the Yuan granted the Sakya sect temporal authority over Tibet. This was statecraft, not piety — it secured the strategic Tibetan plateau and countered Confucian scholar-officials who questioned Mongol legitimacy.

questions.q: Construct a timeline showing how the Red Turban Rebellion (1351) connected to Yellow River floods, Yuan fiscal collapse, and the rise of Zhu Yuanzhang. Identify the critical turning point where Yuan recovery became impossible.
questions.a: Timeline: 1340s — Yellow River shifts course (1344, 1351), massive floods displace millions; 1351 — Yuan orders forced labour for dyke repair, sparking Red Turban uprising (White Lotus sect); 1352 — Zhu Yuanzhang joins Red Turbans; 1356 — Zhu captures Nanjing; 1368 — Zhu proclaims Ming, Yuan flees to steppe. Critical turning point: 1354, when Chancellor Toqto'a was dismissed mid-campaign against rebels due to court factionalism — the Yuan lost its last competent commander and central coordination, making fragmentation inevitable.
